findings.title: Strategy close() shuts down shared FixedQueuePool, breaking rebalance
findings.body: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() calls self.queue_pool.shutdown(), which terminates all worker threads and shuts down the queues. However, the FixedQueuePool is owned by ResultsStrategyFactory and shared across strategy instances. When arroyo triggers a rebalance, it calls close() on the old strategy and then create_with_partitions() to create a new one. The new strategy receives the same (now dead) FixedQueuePool whose workers have all exited. Any messages submitted to the new strategy will sit in the queues forever, never processed, and offsets will never be committed. The pool should either be recreated per strategy, or close() should not shut down the pool (leaving that to the factory's shutdown()).

findings.title: join() does not wait for in-flight work to complete before shutting down
findings.body: The join() method simply calls close(), which sets the shutdown_event, joins the commit thread, and then calls queue_pool.shutdown(). In FixedQueuePool.shutdown(), worker.shutdown is set to True before q.shutdown(immediate=False) is called. A worker that finishes its current item will see self.shutdown == True and exit the while loop without draining remaining items from the queue. This means items that were submitted but not yet processed are silently dropped. The arroyo contract for join() is to wait until all pending work is done. The shutdown sequence should first call q.shutdown(immediate=False) to signal no more items, then let workers drain, and only then set the shutdown flag as a fallback.

findings.title: Unbounded queues provide no backpressure despite docstring claim
findings.body: FixedQueuePool creates queue.Queue() instances without a maxsize argument, making them unbounded. The class docstring states 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up' but this is incorrect—queue.put() on an unbounded queue never blocks. If the Kafka consumer polls messages faster than workers can process them (e.g., due to a slow downstream service), memory usage will grow without bound, potentially causing OOM. A maxsize should be set, or submit() should block/reject when queues are full.

findings.title: A single missing offset permanently blocks all subsequent commits for a partition
findings.body: get_committable_offsets() iterates from the lowest expected offset upward and breaks at the first offset not in all_offsets. If any offset is never added to the tracker (e.g., message.value is not a BrokerValue in the exception path of submit(), or an unexpected error occurs before add_offset is called), that gap can never be filled. All subsequent offsets for that partition become uncommittable forever, causing the consumer to reprocess the entire partition from the last committed offset on every restart. There is no mechanism to detect or recover from such a gap.

findings.title: hash() is randomized per process, so queue assignment is not stable across restarts
findings.body: get_queue_for_group uses Python's built-in hash() on the group key string. Since Python 3.3, string hashing is randomized per process via PYTHONHASHSEED. The docstring says 'consistent hashing' but the assignment is not consistent across process restarts. If ordering guarantees depend on the same group always going to the same queue (e.g., for stateful workers or external side effects keyed by queue), this will break on restart. A deterministic hash like hashlib.md5 or zlib.crc32 should be used instead.

findings.title: Commit loop performs one extra commit iteration after shutdown is signaled
findings.body: In _commit_loop, self.shutdown_event.wait(1.0) returns immediately once the event is set, but the code does not check the return value before proceeding to get_committable_offsets() and commit. This means after close() sets shutdown_event, the loop body executes one more time, potentially calling commit_function after the arroyo Commit object may no longer be valid (e.g., after the consumer has been closed). The wait() return value should be checked and the loop should break if it returns True.

findings.title: queue.ShutDown and Queue.shutdown() require Python 3.13+
findings.body: The code uses queue.ShutDown exception and queue.Queue.shutdown() method, both of which were introduced in Python 3.13. If the project supports earlier Python versions, this will raise AttributeError at runtime. If Python 3.13+ is a hard requirement this is fine, but it should be documented or guarded.

findings.title: _get_partition_lock has a TOCTOU race on partition_locks dictionary
findings.body: _get_partition_lock first calls self.partition_locks.get(partition), and if None, calls self.partition_locks.setdefault(partition, threading.Lock()). While CPython's GIL makes dict.setdefault atomic, two threads could both see None from get() and both call setdefault(). The second setdefault() would return the first thread's lock, so both threads end up with the same lock—this is actually correct behavior. However, the initial get() check is redundant and the pattern is fragile; using only setdefault() would be simpler and equally correct.
